prompt.brief: Design a globally distributed gaming backend for millions of concurrent players with low-latency matchmaking, authoritative game sessions, durable player progress, and regional failover.
successSignals: Separate authoritative per-match state from durable player inventory, ratings, rewards, matchmaking tickets, and telemetry.
Place players and sessions near one another, keep game-loop work bounded, and isolate noisy regions and hot tournaments.
Use a server-authoritative protocol with reconnect tokens, sequence numbers, lag handling, and cheat detection.
Explain matchmaking fairness, party constraints, session migration, regional failure, and durable reward settlement.

functional: Authenticate players, create parties, enqueue matchmaking tickets, and return a match assignment with a region.
Establish real-time game sessions, validate commands, broadcast snapshots, and support reconnect and spectate flows.
Persist inventory, ratings, rewards, bans, and match outcomes with idempotent settlement and auditable events.
nonFunctional: Keep the game loop within a regional tick budget, target p95 command acknowledgement below 100 ms, and matchmaking below 5 seconds.
Scale to millions of concurrent players by sharding sessions and queues by region, mode, and skill bucket.
Do not lose settled rewards or bans; make reconnects, duplicate commands, and match results safe.
Degrade by shedding non-critical telemetry and social reads while protecting authoritative session state.
scaleAssumptions: Support 10 million concurrent connections, 1 million active matches, and bursty launches by region.
Partition by region, game mode, match ID, and player ID; isolate hot tournaments and large parties.
Keep session memory bounded and retain commands, snapshots, settlement records, and telemetry for replay.

dataFlow.title: Create a matchmaking ticket
dataFlow.description: The gateway authenticates the player and party, validates mode and region eligibility, and stores a ticket with a request ID and skill snapshot.

dataFlow.title: Reserve an authoritative session
dataFlow.description: The matchmaker conditionally assigns a session shard and the game service creates a match record before clients receive a join token.

dataFlow.title: Run the regional game loop
dataFlow.description: Clients send sequenced commands to the authoritative game server, which validates them, advances the tick, and broadcasts snapshots or deltas.

dataFlow.title: Settle durable player state
dataFlow.description: Match completion emits a versioned outcome; a settlement worker conditionally applies rewards, ratings, inventory, and bans so duplicate results cannot pay twice.

dataFlow.title: Recover and analyze asynchronously
dataFlow.description: Reconnect state, telemetry, anti-cheat analysis, leaderboards, and analytics consume events independently while session shards handle failover or migration.

deepDives.title: Authoritative sessions and reconnects
points: Keep the simulation authoritative in one regional session shard and replicate snapshots for recovery, not for competing writes.
Use sequence numbers, command IDs, reconnect tokens, and fencing epochs to reject duplicates and stale clients.
Treat rewards and inventory as a separate durable settlement transaction after the match result is finalized.

deepDives.title: Matchmaking fairness and capacity
points: Partition queues by region, mode, skill band, and party size; expand the acceptable skill window only as wait time increases.
Reserve capacity for launches and tournaments, apply admission control, and avoid global coordination in the match hot path.
Keep a replayable ticket and outcome log so matchmaking and settlement can be audited after a regional failure.

deepDives.title: Regional failure and abuse
points: If a region fails, stop new assignments, recover from the latest fenced snapshot, or migrate only at a safe match boundary.
Validate movement and commands server-side, rate-limit reconnects, and feed suspicious behavior to delayed anti-cheat analysis.
Measure tick overruns, command latency, queue wait, disconnect rate, shard saturation, settlement lag, and duplicate rewards.

tradeoffs.title: Strong consistency versus throughput
tradeoffs.recommendation: Strongly protect the business commit and use versioned eventual projections for high-volume reads.
tradeoffs.caution: Making every derived read synchronous increases coordination and tail latency.

tradeoffs.title: Push versus pull processing
tradeoffs.recommendation: Push bounded events to workers and pull durable snapshots on reads or recovery.
tradeoffs.caution: Unbounded fanout or full scans make bursts and hot keys expensive.

tradeoffs.title: Managed service versus custom control
tradeoffs.recommendation: Start with managed primitives where their limits match the access pattern, then isolate replaceable interfaces.
tradeoffs.caution: Provider defaults do not remove the need for quotas, replay, observability, and data lifecycle design.

commonMistakes: Putting all work on the synchronous request path.
Choosing a data store before writing the access patterns and consistency contract.
Ignoring retries, duplicate events, late data, deletion, privacy, or authorization.
Leaving hot partitions, backpressure, stale reads, and recovery unspecified.
Allowing unbounded requests or exports to compete with normal traffic.

followUps.question: What happens when the primary worker is unavailable?
followUps.answer: Acknowledge only after the durable boundary, serve the last acceptable projection, queue retryable work, and replay or reconcile after recovery.

followUps.question: How would you support a tenfold traffic spike?
followUps.answer: Pre-scale partitions, apply admission control and backpressure, isolate hot keys, cache immutable snapshots, and make freshness degradation visible.

followUps.question: How do you verify correctness?
followUps.answer: Use idempotency metrics, version gaps, sampled source-to-projection comparisons, replay tests, and a shadow rebuild before repair.

rubric.description: The answer defines matchmaking, session gameplay, settlement, scale, latency, durability, and failure contracts.
Entities and player/party/session keys support matchmaking, gameplay, settlement, privacy, and lifecycle changes.
Partitioning, cache behavior, queues, backpressure, and hot-key handling are explicit.
Idempotency, replay, recovery, degraded reads, and observability protect committed state.
The candidate can explain Globally distributed gaming backend consistency, push/pull, managed services, and the scale boundary.
